summary: Specifies how a mobile node can move between networks and keep its IP address, with a home agent forwarding its traffic to wherever it currently is. This lets connections keep working as a device roams. It was replaced by RFC 3220.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IP lets a device move between networks while keeping the same IP address, so its existing connections keep working. The device tells a router on its home network where it now is, and that router forwards the incoming traffic through a tunnel to the new location.

questions: how can a device keep its ip address while moving
how does mobile ip registration work
how does a device keep its ip address while moving
subtitle: Letting a device keep its IP address while it moves to another network.

tldr.problem: An IP address says where a device is attached to the Internet, so a device that moves normally has to change its address, which breaks its open connections, or has to drag a host-specific route across the whole network.
tldr.mechanism: Mobile IP keeps the mobile node's home address fixed and gives it a second address, a care-of address, that follows it around. The node registers the care-of address with a home agent, which then intercepts traffic for the home address and tunnels it to the care-of address.
tldr.outcome: The scheme works with no changes to ordinary hosts or routers, and the traffic itself is not encrypted. It was obsoleted by RFC 3220 and updated by RFC 2290.

today: RFC 2002 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3220 and updated by RFC 2290.

sections.title: Why a Moving Device Needs Two Addresses
sections.content:
IP version 4 assumes that a node's address identifies the node's point of attachment to the Internet. A node must therefore be on the network indicated by its address to receive datagrams destined for it. To change its point of attachment without losing the ability to communicate, a node must typically either change its IP address whenever it moves, or have host-specific routes propagated through much of the Internet routing fabric.

Both alternatives are often unacceptable. Changing the address makes it impossible for a node to maintain transport and higher-layer connections when it moves. Propagating host-specific routes has obvious and severe scaling problems, which the RFC connects to the explosive growth in sales of notebook computers.

The protocol places four requirements on the design. A mobile node must be able to communicate with other nodes after changing its link-layer point of attachment without changing its IP address. It must be able to communicate with nodes that implement none of these mobility functions, and no protocol enhancements are required in hosts or routers that are not acting as one of the new entities. All messages used to update another node about a mobile node's location must be authenticated, to protect against remote redirection attacks.

The RFC notes that the link to which a mobile node is directly attached is often wireless, with lower bandwidth and a higher error rate than a wired network, and that such nodes are likely to be battery powered. The number of administrative messages over that link should therefore be minimised, and their size kept as small as reasonably possible.

Mobile IP is intended for movement from one IP subnet to another. It suits movement across homogeneous media as well as heterogeneous media, for example from an Ethernet segment to a wireless LAN, as long as the address stays the same. The RFC describes it as solving the macro mobility management problem, and notes that for micro mobility, such as handoff between wireless transceivers covering a small area, link-layer mechanisms may converge faster with far less overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Every address on the Internet says where a device is plugged in. So a laptop that moves to another network would normally have to change its address, which breaks every connection it has open. Mobile IP avoids that by keeping the old address and forwarding traffic to wherever the device now is.

sections.title: Mobile Nodes, Home Agents and Foreign Agents
sections.content:
Mobile IP introduces three functional entities. A mobile node is a host or router that changes its point of attachment from one network or subnetwork to another. It may change location without changing its address, and may keep communicating with other Internet nodes from any location, as long as link-layer connectivity to a point of attachment is available.

A home agent is a router on the mobile node's home network. It tunnels datagrams for delivery to the mobile node when it is away from home, and it holds the current location information for that node. A foreign agent is a router on the visited network that provides routing services to the mobile node while it is registered there. The foreign agent removes the tunnel and delivers the datagrams that the home agent tunneled, and it may act as the default router for datagrams the mobile node sends.

A mobile node is given a long-term address on its home network, administered in the same way as a permanent address for a stationary host. When it is away from home, a care-of address is associated with it and reflects its current point of attachment. The node uses its home address as the source address of all the datagrams it sends, except for the mobility management messages themselves.

Two kinds of care-of address are defined. A foreign agent care-of address is an address of a foreign agent with which the node has registered, so the foreign agent is the end of the tunnel. This mode is preferred, because many mobile nodes can share the same care-of address and so the limited IPv4 address space is not strained. A co-located care-of address is an externally obtained local address that the node associates with one of its own interfaces, and the node itself ends the tunnel. That mode lets a node work without a foreign agent, but it needs a pool of addresses in the visited network, which is hard to maintain for every subnet a node might visit.

The RFC draws an important distinction between the two ideas. The care-of address is simply the end of the tunnel, and it may be a foreign agent's address or one the node obtained itself. A foreign agent, by contrast, is a mobility agent that provides services to mobile nodes.

The control messages are sent with UDP on the well-known port 434. Two message types are defined, type 1 for a Registration Request and type 3 for a Registration Reply. Mobile IP also reuses the existing ICMP Router Advertisement and Router Solicitation messages for agent discovery, and defines a general extension mechanism in a Type-Length-Value format so that optional information can be carried in those messages. The end of the list of extensions is marked by the total length of the IP datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of device take part. The mobile node is the thing that moves. The home agent is a router on the network the device started from, and it forwards traffic. The foreign agent is a router on the network the device has arrived at, and it delivers the forwarded traffic. A node that gets its own local address does not need a foreign agent at all.

sections.title: Agent Discovery and Move Detection
sections.content:
Agent discovery is how a mobile node works out whether it is on its home network or on a foreign network, and how it detects that it has moved from one network to another. When it is on a foreign network, the same mechanism lets it learn the care-of address being offered by each foreign agent there.

Mobile IP extends ICMP Router Discovery as its primary mechanism. An Agent Advertisement is a router advertisement that carries a Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension, and an Agent Solicitation is identical to a router solicitation except that its IP TTL must be set to 1. The advertisement carries a sequence number counting the messages sent since the agent was initialised, a registration lifetime giving the longest lifetime, in seconds, that the agent will accept in any registration request, a set of flag bits and zero or more care-of addresses.

Those flags describe what the sending agent offers. R means registration with this foreign agent, or another on the same link, is required rather than using a co-located care-of address. B means the foreign agent is busy and will not accept registrations from further mobile nodes. H means the agent offers service as a home agent on the link, and F means it offers service as a foreign agent. M means the agent can receive datagrams tunneled with minimal encapsulation, G means it can receive them with GRE encapsulation, and V means it supports Van Jacobson header compression over the link with any registered mobile node.

At least one of the F and H bits must be set in any agent advertisement, and an advertisement must not set the B bit unless the F bit is also set. An advertisement must include at least one care-of address if the F bit is set.

On the node's side, move detection is the business of noticing that the advertisements have stopped, or that their sequence numbers have moved on. The RFC gives two algorithms for it. Algorithm 1 uses the expiration of the agent advertisement lifetime. Algorithm 2 uses a sequence number carried in the advertisement, together with a timer, and the RFC explains how sequence numbers are compared and how rollover is handled.
sections.plainLanguage: The device listens for regular announcements from the routers on whatever network it is on. When the announcements stop arriving, or their sequence numbers jump, the device knows it has moved and starts looking for a new address.

sections.title: Registration and the Mobility Binding
sections.content:
Registration is how a mobile node tells its home agent where it is. The node uses it to ask for forwarding services when it visits a foreign network, to give its home agent its current care-of address, to renew a registration that is about to expire, and to deregister when it comes home. Registration creates or modifies a mobility binding at the home agent, associating the home address with the care-of address for a stated lifetime.

Two procedures exist. If the node is registering a foreign agent care-of address, it must register through that foreign agent, and four messages are exchanged: the node sends a Registration Request to the foreign agent, the foreign agent relays it to the home agent, the home agent replies to the foreign agent granting or denying the request, and the foreign agent relays the reply to the node. If the node registers directly with its home agent, which it must do when it uses a co-located care-of address and has no foreign agent to use, only two messages are needed.

The Registration Request is a UDP datagram to port 434. Its header carries a type byte, the home address, the home agent address and the care-of address, followed by an identification field and then extensions. The registration request also has flag bits. S means the node wants simultaneous bindings, so that a copy of each datagram is tunneled to each active care-of address. B asks the home agent to send a Registration Reply to the node itself rather than to a foreign agent. D, M and G request that a copy of the Registration Request be returned in the reply for diagnostic purposes, and that minimal or GRE encapsulation be used.

Registration messages between a mobile node and its home agent must be authenticated with the Mobile-Home Authentication Extension, which immediately follows all the non-authentication extensions. The extension type numbers are 32 for Mobile-Home Authentication, 33 for Mobile-Foreign Authentication and 34 for Foreign-Home Authentication. The foreign agent uses the low-order 32 bits of the identification field, together with the mobile node's home address, to match a request with its reply, and the mobile node must check that those bits come back unchanged.

When the lifetime of a binding expires without another valid request, the home agent deletes that binding, but it must retain any other simultaneous bindings it holds for the same node. The home agent must not send a registration reply simply because a binding has expired.
sections.plainLanguage: The device tells its home router where it now is, and the home router remembers that for a set time, usually a couple of minutes. The device renews the message before it runs out, and the router forgets the device if the renewal stops arriving.

sections.title: Tunneling and Routing
sections.content:
Home agents and foreign agents must support tunneling datagrams with IP in IP encapsulation, and any mobile node using a co-located care-of address must support receiving datagrams tunneled that way. Minimal encapsulation and GRE encapsulation are alternatives that may optionally be supported.

When the mobile node is registered away from home, the home agent examines the destination address of every arriving datagram. If it matches the home address of a registered mobile node, the home agent tunnels the datagram to the node's currently registered care-of address. If the home agent supports the optional capability of multiple simultaneous mobility bindings, it tunnels a copy to each care-of address in the binding list.

The datagram travels inside another IP datagram, so the home address stays hidden from the routers in between. At the far end, either the foreign agent or the mobile node itself removes the outer header and delivers the original datagram. A foreign agent checks the inner destination address against its visitor list before forwarding, and if it does not match it must not forward the datagram unmodified, because a routing loop would likely result; the datagram should be silently discarded, and no ICMP Destination Unreachable is sent. The foreign agent must route datagrams it receives from registered mobile nodes, at minimum by verifying the IP header checksum, decrementing the time to live, recomputing the checksum and forwarding to a default router.

On the home network the home agent attracts traffic for its mobile nodes using proxy and gratuitous ARP. The RFC notes that ARP is not authenticated and can potentially be used to steal another host's traffic, and that the use of gratuitous ARP brings with it all of the risks of using ARP.

Datagrams sent by the mobile node generally reach their destination by ordinary IP routing and do not pass through the home agent at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic for the device arrives at the home router as if the device were still there. The router wraps each datagram in another one, sends that to the address the device gave it, and the wrapping is stripped off at the far end. Other routers on the path see only the outer address, so the home address stays private.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mobile computing environment differs from the ordinary one. Mobile computers are often connected through wireless links, which are particularly vulnerable to passive eavesdropping, active replay attacks and other active attacks.

Home agents and mobile nodes must be able to perform authentication. The default algorithm is keyed MD5 with a 128-bit key, used in prefix and suffix mode, and the foreign agent must also support keyed MD5 with key sizes of 128 bits or greater and manual key distribution. Other algorithms, modes, key distribution methods and key sizes may also be supported.

The registration protocol causes a mobile node's traffic to be tunneled to its care-of address, and that is a significant vulnerability if the registration is not authenticated, because remote redirection of a registration is widely understood to be a security problem in the Internet. The RFC also notes that the Address Resolution Protocol is not authenticated and can potentially be used to steal another host's traffic.

Key management is difficult in the absence of a network key management protocol, which is why messages with the foreign agent are not all required to be authenticated. In a commercial environment it may be important to authenticate all messages between the foreign agent and the home agent, so that billing is possible and so that service providers do not serve users who are not legitimate customers.

For the keyed MD5 key to be useful it must be both secret and pseudo-random, and any nonces used for replay protection must be chosen carefully. All mobile nodes and home agents must implement timestamp-based replay protection, in which the sender puts the current time into the identification field and the receiver checks that it is close to its own time, which requires the two nodes to have adequately synchronised clocks. They may also implement nonce-based replay protection. Whatever method is used, the low-order 32 bits of the identification must be copied unchanged from the request to the reply.

On privacy, the RFC says that users with sensitive data should use mechanisms outside its scope, such as encryption, and that users concerned about traffic analysis should consider link encryption. If absolute location privacy is wanted, the mobile node can create a tunnel to its home agent, so that datagrams to correspondent nodes appear to come from the home network and it is harder to pinpoint the node's location.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering where you are is a target for anyone who wants to redirect your traffic, so the message has to be signed. The RFC signs it with an old hash function, keyed MD5, and checks the timestamp in it so that a captured registration cannot be replayed later.

viz.caption: The two kinds of care-of address

left.title: Foreign agent care-of address
left.desc: The address belongs to the foreign agent, which ends the tunnel and hands over the datagram. Many mobile nodes can share one address.

right.title: Co-located care-of address
right.desc: The address is obtained locally and the mobile node ends the tunnel itself, so no foreign agent is needed.

viz.caption: The flags in a Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension

items.label: Registration required
items.desc: Registration with this foreign agent is required rather than using a co-located care-of address.

items.label: Busy
items.desc: The foreign agent will not accept registrations from additional mobile nodes.

items.label: Home agent
items.desc: This agent offers service as a home agent on the link.

items.label: Foreign agent
items.desc: This agent offers service as a foreign agent on the link.

items.label: Minimal encapsulation
items.desc: This agent can receive tunneled datagrams that use minimal encapsulation.

items.label: GRE encapsulation
items.desc: This agent can receive tunneled datagrams that use GRE encapsulation.

items.label: Van Jacobson header compression
items.desc: This agent supports Van Jacobson header compression over the link with any registered mobile node.
